The size of the step, , is the value of scarce storage capacity in that hour. This is the week 4 congestion argument moved from space to time: a congested line separates two nodal prices by its multiplier, a full or empty battery separates two hourly values of stored energy by its multiplier.

Deriving the KKT conditions of the toy step by step

The table above states the multipliers; this subsection derives them. Two simplifications make the toy transparent: no losses () and no minimum end level (, so the last-hour energy bounds are the ordinary and is the multiplier of ). With , , , and , the problem of section 3 is:

Step 1 — Lagrangian of the toy

Minimise the negative profit; equality multipliers free, inequality multipliers , every inequality written as . With and the Lagrangian of section 5 becomes:

Each appears in two dynamics terms: with in its own hour and with in the next one. That is where the coupling across hours enters the KKT conditions.

Step 2 — the KKT conditions of the toy

Differentiate with respect to each of the twelve primal variables, then add complementarity and feasibility:

Twelve stationarity equations, sixteen complementarity products, and a primal point. Because the problem is an LP that satisfies Slater's condition, any pair (primal, multipliers) that satisfies all of them is optimal — so it is enough to start from the hand solution of section 2 and find multipliers that fit.

Step 3 — the primal solution, and which bounds bind

From section 2: , , . Complementarity – says that a multiplier can only be non-zero when its bound is tight. Reading the schedule hour by hour:

The partial actions are the key: in hour 2 (charging 5 of 10 kW) and hour 3 (discharging 5 of 10 kW) both power multipliers of the active direction vanish, and or collapses to . These are the marginal hours; everything else follows from them.

Step 4 — hour 3 sets , hour 2 sets

Interpretation. In a marginal hour the battery is indifferent between acting one kW more or less, so the price it faces is the value of a kWh inside the battery. After hour 3, one more kWh in the battery would be sold in hour 3 itself at 60 — not in hour 4 at 80, because hour 4 is already at its power limit. After hour 2, one more kWh could have been bought in hour 2 at 30, so that is what a stored kWh is worth then.

Step 5 — propagates across the hours

Interpretation. While the state of charge is strictly inside its bounds, a kWh can be carried from one hour to the next at no cost, so its value cannot change: and . The value can only jump where the battery is full or empty, and the jump is the multiplier of that bound. At the end of hour 2 the battery is full: the value steps up from 30 to 60, and is what one more kWh of room would have been worth in that hour — buy it at 30, sell it at 60. At the end of hour 4 the battery is empty and the horizon ends: is what the bound costs — one more kWh available after hour 4 would have been sold at 60 in hour 3, the last hour with spare selling power.

Step 6 — the saturated hours: the power rents

Interpretation. In hour 1 the battery buys at 20 a kWh worth 30 and would like to buy more; the power limit stops it, and DKK/kW is the rent of that limit — what one more kW of charging power would earn in that hour. In hour 4 it sells at 80 a kWh worth 60: DKK/kW is the rent of the discharging limit. This is exactly the week 4 reading of on a generator's capacity, in both directions.

Step 7 — the idle directions: multipliers of the lower bounds

The remaining stationarity equations are those of the direction the battery does not use in each hour; they determine the multipliers of :

Interpretation. A multiplier of is the loss that the first kW in that direction would cause. Discharging in hour 1 would sell at 20 a kWh worth 30: . Charging in hour 4 would buy at 80 a kWh worth 60: . In the marginal hours 2 and 3 the unused direction costs nothing at the margin (): the battery is indifferent, which is what ‘marginal’ means.

Step 8 — check, and conclude

Every multiplier found is non-negative and every is finite, so holds; the primal point satisfies –; the sixteen complementarity products are zero by construction. All KKT conditions hold, and since KKT are sufficient for an LP, the hand schedule is optimal and these are its multipliers. They are also unique here: no partial action sits at a bound, so no equation had a free choice. (That is not always so — at kWh the optimum is at a kink and can be reported as 0 or 30 depending on the vertex the solver returns; the two one-sided re-solves settle it.)

Two analogies with the economic dispatch: the marginal hour, and congestion across hours

Week 4 gave two readings of a multiplier in the economic dispatch. The market price is the cost of the marginal unit, the one dispatched strictly between its bounds; and a difference in price between two areas is the multiplier of the line between them, whose capacity earns a congestion rent. Both readings carry over to the battery once hours are read as areas, the market in each hour as that area's generators and loads, and the state of charge as the line that carries energy from one hour to the next. The multipliers of the power bounds then play the first role and the multipliers of the energy bounds the second.

Analogy 1 — the marginal hour is the marginal generator (or the marginal flexible load)

In the economic dispatch, a generator with cost and bounds has the stationarity condition and three regimes: not dispatched (, ), marginal (, both multipliers zero, so ) and fully loaded (, , a rent). The marginal unit sets the price because it is the only one that can respond at the margin: if the load consumed one more MWh, that unit would produce it, at cost ; if the load consumed one less, that unit would back down. The fully loaded units cannot produce more and the undispatched ones will not produce at this price. A flexible load is the mirror image: , and a partially served load sets — if one more MWh became available, that load would take it, and it is worth .

Now read hour as an area of its own, in which the battery can buy or sell at up to , and read the stored kWh as the commodity being traded, at price . and are then exactly the generator's and the load's conditions. A discharging hour produces from the stock: it earns and uses up a kWh worth , so its “cost” is and reads (no losses). A charging hour consumes into the stock: it pays for a kWh worth , so its “utility” is and reads . The three regimes follow:

What “the marginal hour sets ” means. Suppose one extra kWh appeared in the battery at the end of hour — a gift. Some hour has to change its schedule to accommodate it, and it can only be an hour with slack in both directions: a marginal hour. That hour's price is what the gift is worth, and that is . In the toy, a kWh appearing after hour 3 is sold in hour 3 itself, one more kWh at 60: . It is not sold in hour 4 at 80, because hour 4 already discharges at — like a fully loaded generator, it cannot respond. A kWh appearing after hour 1 is not sold at all: hour 2 simply buys one kWh less, saving 30: . Hour 1 cannot respond (at ), and hours 3–4 cannot receive it because the battery is full at the end of hour 2 (analogy 2). Taking a kWh out is symmetric: the marginal hour compensates, hour 3 sells one less (−60), hour 2 buys one more (−30). This is the week 4 statement “one more MWh of load is served by the marginal unit; one less backs it down”, with the stored kWh as the load.

So the value of stored energy in hour is the price of the marginal hour of the plateau that belongs to, whichever direction that hour acts in — not the price of the hour in which the energy eventually gets sold. Sections 2 and 6 state the same thing as a merit order of price spreads; the figure draws it as two merit orders of the stored kWh: in hours 1–2 the charging hours supply the 15 kWh that fill the battery (h1 fully loaded at 20, h2 marginal at 30), in hours 3–4 the discharging hours take them (h4 fully served at 80, h3 marginal at 60). With losses the marginal condition becomes for charging and for discharging — a generator whose “fuel” is stock and whose efficiency is .

Analogy 2 — a full or empty battery is a congested line between two hours

In the economic dispatch with ATC, two areas and are linked by a line with multiplier , and stationarity in the flow gives . While the line has spare capacity both multipliers are zero and the two areas share one price. When it is congested from to , the price difference is the multiplier of the capacity constraint — the value of one more MW of line — and the line earns the congestion rent : it buys MWh on the cheap side and sells them on the dear side.

The dynamics carry energy from hour to hour , and the state of charge is the flow on that link. The link has capacity in the forward direction and capacity 0 in the backward direction: time runs one way, the battery cannot discharge today what it will charge tomorrow. With this reading, is the ATC condition:

is , the multiplier of the forward capacity ; is , the multiplier of the backward capacity 0. While the link is uncongested and the two hours share one value, : energy moves freely across, and the whole plateau is one “area” with one marginal hour. When the battery is full at the end of hour , the forward link is congested: the hours after are the dear side, the battery would carry more if it could, and steps up by — the value of one more kWh of capacity on this link. The battery earns on it exactly what a congested line earns: it bought kWh on the cheap side and sells them on the dear side, a rent of . In the toy the link from hour 2 to hour 3 is congested, , and the rent is 30 × 15 = 450 DKK. When the battery is empty at the end of hour , the backward link is the congested one: the hours before are the dear side, the battery would like to carry energy back from the cheap hours after and cannot, and steps down by . That link has zero capacity, so its rent is zero — but the multiplier still says what a kWh moved back in time would be worth; at , in the toy is what one more kWh available after hour 4 would have earned before it.

Moving energy across time is moving it across space. An interconnector buys in the cheap area and sells in the dear one; a battery buys in the cheap hours and sells in the dear ones. Both are arbitrage limited by a capacity, both earn a rent equal to the price difference times the capacity, and both narrow the very price difference they live on when they are large — which is why the price-taker assumption of section 3 matters. The one asymmetry is direction: a line can be congested either way, the storage link only forwards. Hence the value of stored energy can only rise at a full hour and only fall at an empty one.

Left: a congested line between two areas of the week 4 model; the price difference is the multiplier of the ATC constraint and the line earns it on every MW of capacity. Right: the toy read the same way. Each hour is an area with its own price and value ; the arrows are the state of charge carried to the next hour. The link h2 → h3 is at its capacity : it is the only place where changes, and its rent DKK is the battery's congestion rent across hours; with the two power rents (300 DKK) it accounts for the whole profit.

The last remark is general. By strong duality the optimal profit equals the dual objective, which contains only the constants of the problem and their multipliers:

A price-taking battery earns nothing but rents: the congestion rent across hours (energy capacity × the jumps of at the full hours), the capacity rents of its power limits (the scarcity rent of a fully loaded generator, in both directions), the value of the stock it starts with, minus what the end requirement costs. Toy: 750 = 15 × 30 + 10 × (10 + 20). Class day of section 7: 2 680 = 25 × 82 + 10 × 63. This is the week 4 identity that the merchandising surplus of the dispatch equals the sum of the congestion rents, and a generator's profit the sum of its capacity rents — and it is why the multiplier sums of section 7 are the sizing signals: each is the rent that one more unit of the corresponding capacity would collect.

Why the energy bounds split the day, and the power bounds pick the marginal hour

The two kinds of bounds play the two roles of the dispatch, and neither can play the other's.

  • The energy bounds are the line capacities. They appear only in , the condition that links to . They decide where the value of stored energy can change — at a full or empty hour — and therefore how the day splits into plateaus of constant , the “areas” of the temporal network. Their multipliers , are congestion rents per kWh of capacity: the price difference between two consecutive areas. A power bound cannot do this: it never enters , so it cannot make jump — it does not stop energy from being carried to the next hour.
  • The power bounds are the generator capacities inside an area. They appear only in –, the conditions that link to hour by hour. Within a plateau they decide which hour is marginal — the one whose power is strictly between 0 and — and that hour's price becomes the value of the whole plateau; the hours at are inframarginal and earn per kW. An energy bound cannot do this: it says nothing about how much power moves within an hour, so it cannot make an hour marginal or tie to .
  • Put together: within a plateau, equals the price of its marginal hour; across a full or empty hour, jumps by the congestion rent per kWh. When a plateau has no marginal hour — every hour at or idle, as at kWh in the toy — is pinned only to an interval, exactly as the dispatch price is undetermined when the load falls precisely at a generator's capacity; that is the kink case of section 7, where the multipliers are not unique.
